reasoning: Unresponsive patient is unable to protect airway or communicate; unresponsiveness alone meets ESI-1 criteria (immediate life-saving intervention required).
High-risk context: suicidal history + found unresponsive + alcohol bottles + multiple empty pill bottles suggests acute overdose or poisoning.

Vital signs NOT RECORDED is itself a critical safety gap; inability to assess airway patency, breathing effort, perfusion status, and oxygenation in unresponsive patient is dangerous and mandates immediate intervention.

Age 17 (adolescent) with documented suicidality represents extremely high-risk population for completed suicide attempt; intentional self-harm with mixed substances (alcohol + unknown pills) is presumed until proven otherwise.

Unknown pill bottles prevent pharmacokinetic prediction; some toxins (anticholinergic, sedative-hypnotic, opioid combinations) cause rapid respiratory depression and require emergent airway management.

Unresponsiveness + suspected polysubstance ingestion = requires immediate: (1) airway assessment & protection if needed, (2) blood glucose check, (3) naloxone if opioid suspected, (4) full vital signs including SpO2, (5) stat labs/toxicology, (6) ICU-level monitoring.
No prior medical record limits ability to differentiate accidental from intentional; must treat as worst-case (active overdose requiring resuscitation).
red_flags: Unresponsiveness — cannot maintain airway or respond to commands
Presumed acute polysubstance ingestion (alcohol + unknown pills)
History of suicidality with behavioral act (found unconscious at scene)
Vitals not recorded — cannot assess hypoxia, hypotension, respiratory depression, or bradycardia
Empty pill bottles unidentified — unknown toxin, dose, time of ingestion
First-time patient — no baseline mental status or comorbidity data
Adolescent age group — high-risk for completed suicide; atypical presentations common
Opioid combination suspected (alcohol + pills) — respiratory depression and aspiration risk
